course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: Land-Based Empires
unit.description: Study how gunpowder, administration, and religion helped land-based empires expand and hold power across Eurasia and Africa.

firstTopic.title: Empires Expand
firstTopic.summary: How gunpowder weapons, military organization, and rivalries shaped the growth of the Ottoman, Safavid, Mughal, Qing, and Songhai states.

topic.title: Empires: Belief Systems
topic.summary: How the Protestant and Catholic reformations, the Sunni and Shi'a rivalry, and the rise of Sikhism changed belief systems from 1450 to 1750.

framework.name: InSPECT
framework.title: Use InSPECT to choose your evidence

themes.title: Interactions of humans with the environment
themes.question: How did geography, crops, resources, or disease shape choices?
themes.example: Andean terraces made steep slopes more usable for farming.

themes.title: Social interactions and organization
themes.question: Who had status, opportunities, or obligations?
themes.example: Examination preparation favored families that could afford education.

themes.title: Political systems and governance
themes.question: How did rulers gain authority and administer territory?
themes.example: Song officials carried imperial decisions into local government.

themes.title: Economic systems
themes.question: How were goods produced, exchanged, taxed, or distributed?
themes.example: Mali drew revenue from commerce through its territory.

themes.title: Cultural developments and interactions
themes.question: How did beliefs, learning, and artistic practices influence society?
themes.example: Buddhist monasteries connected religious practice with education.

themes.title: Technology and innovation
themes.question: What techniques or tools changed what people could do?
themes.example: Inca roads and knotted records helped officials coordinate resources.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Martin Luther, German monk and professor of theology, Disputation on the Power and Efficacy of Indulgences (the Ninety-five Theses), Wittenberg, 1517
stimulusBlocks.citation: Works of Martin Luther, trans. and ed. Adolph Spaeth, L. D. Reed, Henry Eyster Jacobs, et al. (Philadelphia: A. J. Holman Company, 1915), vol. 1, pp. 29–38, theses 21, 27–28, 36, 50, and 86. Project Gutenberg eBook #274.
stimulusBlocks.note: Indulgences were grants from the Church said to reduce punishment for sins. “They preach man” means they preach human teaching rather than God's. Bracketed words are the translators'. Thesis 86 is one of several questions Luther says ordinary believers were asking.
stimulusBlocks.text:
21. Therefore those preachers of indulgences are in error, who say that by the pope's indulgences a man is freed from every penalty, and saved; . . .

27. They preach man who say that so soon as the penny jingles into the money-box, the soul flies out [of purgatory].

28. It is certain that when the penny jingles into the money-box, gain and avarice can be increased, but the result of the intercession of the Church is in the power of God alone. . . .

36. Every truly repentant Christian has a right to full remission of penalty and guilt, even without letters of pardon. . . .

50. Christians are to be taught that if the pope knew the exactions of the pardon-preachers, he would rather that St. Peter's church should go to ashes, than that it should be built up with the skin, flesh and bones of his sheep. . . .

86. Again:--"Why does not the pope, whose wealth is to-day greater than the riches of the richest, build just this one church of St. Peter with his own money, rather than with the money of poor believers?"

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 3.3, KC-4.1.VI.i: the Protestant Reformation marked a break with established Christian traditions, and the Catholic Reformation responded
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the Catholic Reformation, 1540–1600
stimulusBlocks.text:
The Catholic Church answered the Protestant challenge in several ways. The Council of Trent, which met between 1545 and 1563, reaffirmed Catholic teachings on the sacraments and the authority of Church tradition, while ordering bishops to correct abuses such as the sale of church offices. New religious orders, especially the Society of Jesus, or Jesuits, founded in 1540, opened schools and sent missionaries to Asia, Africa, and the Americas.

The result was not reunion. Europe remained divided between Catholic and Protestant states, and religious difference fed wars such as the Thirty Years' War of 1618 to 1648.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 3.3, KC-4.1.VI.ii: within Islam, the Sunni–Shi'a split was widened by the political rivalry between the Ottoman and Safavid empires
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the Ottoman–Safavid rivalry, 1501–1639
stimulusBlocks.text:
When Ismail I founded the Safavid dynasty in Persia in 1501, he declared Twelver Shi'ism the official religion and pressed his largely Sunni subjects to convert. The neighboring Ottomans, who were Sunni, saw Safavid preachers among Anatolian tribes as a threat. Sultan Selim I defeated Ismail at the Battle of Chaldiran in 1514, where Ottoman cannons and muskets overwhelmed Safavid cavalry.

The two empires fought repeatedly until a treaty in 1639 set a lasting border. Their rivalry turned a religious difference into a political boundary, and Persia remained mostly Shi'a while Ottoman lands remained mostly Sunni.

The passage says Ottoman firearms overwhelmed the Safavid cavalry.
The Safavids remained Shi'a.
questions.distinguisher: Firearms decided the battle, but they were Ottoman weapons; the Safavids relied mainly on cavalry.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 3.3, KC-4.1.VI.iii: some belief systems, such as Sikhism, developed as a blend of existing traditions
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the origins of Sikhism, c. 1500–1604
stimulusBlocks.text:
Sikhism began in the Punjab region of northern India with Guru Nanak, who lived from 1469 to 1539. Nanak taught devotion to one God and rejected the idea that ritual, caste, or religious labels made a person closer to the divine. His followers ate together in community kitchens open to all, regardless of caste.

Scholars see connections between Nanak's teachings and both Hindu bhakti devotion and Islamic Sufism, which were widespread in the region. Yet his successors built distinct institutions, and in 1604 the fifth Guru compiled the Adi Granth, the Sikh scripture.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 3.3 key concept: Sunni–Shi'a divisions shaped the rivalry between the Ottoman and Safavid empires
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the early Safavid state and its conflict with the Ottomans, 1501–1639
stimulusBlocks.text:
In 1501 Shah Ismail founded the Safavid dynasty in Persia and made Twelver Shi'ism the state religion, even though most of his subjects were Sunni. He brought Shi'i scholars from Lebanon and Iraq to teach the faith, and Safavid rulers pressed their subjects to convert.

The Ottoman sultans were Sunni and saw the Safavids as both heretics and a military threat. In 1514 an Ottoman army armed with muskets and cannon defeated Safavid cavalry at Chaldiran and briefly occupied the Safavid capital of Tabriz. The two empires fought over their borders for more than a century.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 3.3 key concept: Sunni–Shi'a divisions shaped the rivalry between the Ottoman and Safavid empires
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the early Safavid state and its conflict with the Ottomans, 1501–1639
stimulusBlocks.text:
In 1501 Shah Ismail founded the Safavid dynasty in Persia and made Twelver Shi'ism the state religion, even though most of his subjects were Sunni. He brought Shi'i scholars from Lebanon and Iraq to teach the faith, and Safavid rulers pressed their subjects to convert.

The Ottoman sultans were Sunni and saw the Safavids as both heretics and a military threat. In 1514 an Ottoman army armed with muskets and cannon defeated Safavid cavalry at Chaldiran and briefly occupied the Safavid capital of Tabriz. The two empires fought over their borders for more than a century.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 3.3 key concept: the Catholic Reformation responded to Protestant challenges through reform and missionary work
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the Catholic Reformation, 1540–1600
stimulusBlocks.text:
In response to the Protestant Reformation, the Catholic Church held the Council of Trent between 1545 and 1563. The council reaffirmed teachings that Protestants rejected, including the authority of the pope and the value of both faith and good works. It also ended the sale of indulgences, required bishops to live in their dioceses, and ordered seminaries to train priests.

The Society of Jesus, founded by Ignatius of Loyola and approved in 1540, ran schools across Europe and sent missionaries to Asia and the Americas, such as Francis Xavier in India and Japan. Catholic rulers, including Philip II of Spain, also used the Inquisition to suppress heresy.
